The Yellowcheek (Elopichthys bambusa) is a large piscivorous cyprinid native to major river systems of eastern Asia. Field surveys indicate that newly hatched larvae emerge from pelagic eggs with a minute wet weight of approximately 0.001 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.001 grams], reflecting an egg diameter of roughly 1.25 millimeters. This exceptionally low birth mass underscores the altricial state of the prolarvae, which depend entirely on a yolk reserve during the first days of exogenous feeding onset. As the yolk-sac larva transitions to active feeding, rapid somatic growth ensues. Juvenile specimens sampled in the Amur River basin exhibit a near-exponential increase in body mass during the initial growing season, a pattern characteristic of predatory teleosts occupying a high trophic level. The species' life-history strategy is further defined by its considerable ultimate total length; the largest verified individual measured 200 centimeters [Li = 200 centimeters] from snout to caudal fin tip. This size class places Elopichthys bambusa among the largest-bodied cyprinids globally, competing in length only with a handful of other Asian freshwater giants such as Catlocarpio siamensis.

Reproductive maturation in Yellowcheek is tied to a specific body length rather than a strict chronological age; gonad development accelerates once individuals surpass approximately 89.9 centimeters [Lp = approximately 89.9 centimeters] in total length. This threshold marks the transition to the puberty stage, after which the HPG axis becomes fully activated and vitellogenesis commences in gravid females. At this developmental milestone, the corresponding body mass is considerable; field-caught specimens at the onset of sexual maturation typically exhibit a wet weight near 6580 grams [Wwp = 6580 grams]. This weight at puberty represents a substantial energetic investment in somatic growth prior to any allocation of resources toward oocyte production. The relationship between length and weight in this species exhibits a strong allometric component, with adult females generally attaining a greater mass than males of comparable fork length. Spawning migrations are triggered by seasonal flood pulses, which provide the necessary hydrological cues for oviposition over vegetated floodplains.

The maximum recorded lifespan for Yellowcheek has been estimated from scale annuli and otolith increment analyses, yielding a longevity of approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] under the thermal regime of a typical temperate river system at 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan, uncommon among fast-growing cyprinids, is consistent with an iteroparous reproductive strategy in which adults spawn repeatedly across several seasons. Senescent individuals collected in the lower reaches of the Yangtze River show progressive deterioration of gonadal tissue and reduced gamete quality, indicative of reproductive senescence in the latter portion of the lifespan. The ability to survive for over a decade allows multiple spawning events, which buffers the population against recruitment failures in years with unfavorable hydrologic conditions. Comparative data from related cyprinid species suggest that the lifespan of Elopichthys bambusa is near the upper boundary for the family, exceeded only by certain carps and barbines in controlled environments.

Under captive conditions designed to simulate optimal thermal conditions at 16 °C [T = 16 °C], a single female Yellowcheek has been documented to produce approximately 3,364,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 3,364,000 eggs per spawning event], with about 1 spawning event occurring per year. This extraordinarily high fecundity per event, while plausible only under continuous captive conditions with unlimited food, implies a cumulative reproductive potential that is among the highest documented for any freshwater teleost. The batch-spawning strategy, characterized by the release of large clutches at annual intervals, contrasts sharply with the multiple spawning pulses observed in many other large-bodied cyprinids. Field studies in the Ussuri River indicate that wild populations likely spawn at a considerably lower frequency, constrained by seasonal temperature windows and prey availability. The experimental data were collected from a broodstock maintained at the Heilongjiang River Fisheries Research Institute under controlled photoperiod and feeding regimes, providing the maximum reproduction rate of 3,364,000 eggs per spawning event [Ri = of 3,364,000 eggs per spawning event] at 16 °C [T = 16 °C].

The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adult Yellowcheek has been estimated from length-weight regressions applied to the largest recorded individuals, yielding an asymptotic mass of approximately 76624 grams [Wwi = approximately 76624 grams]. This formidable body size, exceeding 76 kilograms, classifies Elopichthys bambusa as a megafaunal element of East Asian freshwater ecosystems and a top predator in riverine food webs. Stomach content analyses from adult specimens reveal a diet dominated by other cyprinids, including Pseudorasbora parva and Hemiculter leucisculus, as well as occasional predation on juvenile conspecifics. The species' rapid growth trajectory, coupled with its high metabolic demands, necessitates a foraging strategy centered on ambush predation in turbid, slow-moving waters where submerged structure provides cover. Conservation concerns have emerged in recent decades due to overfishing, dam construction, and habitat fragmentation, which collectively impede the long-distance spawning migrations required for successful recruitment. Current population trends in the Amur and Yangtze drainages indicate a marked decline, prompting listing as a protected species in several Chinese provinces.
